L8  /  Pathological basis of oral & systemic disease

Cardiovascular & Blood Disorders

From the endothelium outwards: atherosclerosis, hypertension, heart failure and ischaemic heart disease, then haemostasis and the bleeding disorders you will manage in the chair.

Lecturer
Dr Joseph Ryan
Sections
15
Core reading
Underwood’s Ch. 13 & 23
Key link
Endocarditis & dental bacteraemia
01

Normal arterial structure and ageing

Three layers, and what time does to them.

Structure

Three layers

  • Arteries composed of intima, media, adventitia
  • Internal/external elastic laminae present
  • Media varies in muscularity depending on vessel size
  • Vasa vasorum supply the outer vessel wall
  • Endothelium = critical regulator of vascular health
Ageing

Two changes

  • Progressive intimal fibrosis — collagen and ECM accumulate, smooth muscle cells are lost, the intima thickens and stiffens
  • Medial elastic fibre degeneration — elastin fragments and is replaced by dense collagen, reducing compliance and recoil
Why old arteries give a wide pulse pressure

Arterial stiffening → widened pulse pressure. A compliant aorta absorbs the systolic ejection and releases it in diastole. A stiff one cannot, so systolic pressure rises and diastolic falls. This is why isolated systolic hypertension is common in older adults — it is a mechanical consequence of losing elastin.

The endothelium is the recurring character

Note it is called the critical regulator of vascular health. Endothelial injury starts atherosclerosis, endothelial dysfunction drives hypertension and diabetic vascular disease, and endothelial exposure of collagen triggers haemostasis. Almost everything in this lecture begins at the endothelium.

From the lecture slides
02

Atherosclerosis: pathogenesis

Five steps from a damaged endothelium to a fibrous cap.

Atherosclerosis

A chronic inflammatory, lipid-driven disease of large and medium arteries, affecting elastic and muscular arteries (aorta, coronary, carotid, iliac). It is progressive, multifactorial and lifelong. Central mechanism: endothelial injury + lipid accumulation.

  1. Endothelial injury / dysfunction
    Mechanical stress (hypertension), toxins (smoking), hyperglycaemia (diabetes), hyperlipidaemia, turbulent flow. Shear stress damage is worst at bifurcations.
  2. LDL infiltration and oxidation in the intima
    Oxidised LDL is chemotactic, pro-inflammatory and cytotoxic, and stimulates expression of adhesion molecules (VCAM-1, ICAM-1).
  3. Monocyte adhesion → macrophages → foam cells
    Macrophages engulf oxidised LDL. Foam cells accumulate to form fatty streaks and release cytokines that amplify inflammation.
  4. Smooth muscle cell migration and ECM deposition
    Smooth muscle cells migrate from media to intima and produce collagen, elastin and proteoglycans.
  5. Fibrous cap formation over the lipid core
    The cap stabilises the plaque but may thin over time. The necrotic core contains dead cells, cholesterol esters and debris.
This is chronic inflammation, in an artery

Every element is from Lecture 3B: VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 adhesion (the same molecules as leukocyte emigration in L3A), monocytes becoming macrophages, macrophages releasing cytokines, and fibroblast-like cells laying down collagen. Atherosclerosis is chronic inflammation where the indigestible agent is oxidised LDL.

Why do atherosclerotic plaques form preferentially at arterial bifurcations?

Because of shear stress damage from turbulent flow. Laminar flow is protective for the endothelium; at branch points flow becomes disturbed, injuring the endothelium and increasing permeability to LDL. Since endothelial injury is step 1 of the whole process, the sites of greatest mechanical disturbance are where plaques begin.

03

Plaque structure and vulnerability

Which plaques kill — and it is not the biggest ones.

Components of an atheromatous plaque

Fibrous capCollagen-rich layer stabilising the plaque, produced by smooth muscle cells
Lipid-rich necrotic coreCholesterol, cholesterol esters, cell debris; site of intense inflammation
Foam cells & macrophagesMajor producers of inflammatory cytokines; contribute to core expansion
CalcificationProgresses with age; may stiffen the vessel and impair vasomotion
NeovascularisationFragile microvessels → risk of intraplaque haemorrhage

Characteristics of vulnerable (unstable) plaques

Thin fibrous cap — prone to rupture Large lipid core — increased mechanical stress High inflammatory infiltrate — MMPs weaken the cap Less calcified, softer plaques — structurally fragile
The counter-intuitive point

A vulnerable plaque is softer and less calcified, not harder. The dangerous plaque is often not the one causing the tightest stenosis — a lipid-rich, thin-capped, inflamed plaque may barely narrow the lumen and still rupture and kill. That is why a patient can have a fatal MI with no preceding angina.

Clinical consequences

Gradual

Progressive stenosis → chronic ischaemia

Coronary → stable angina. Peripheral → claudication. Mesenteric → postprandial pain.

Sudden

Plaque rupture → acute thrombosis

Acute coronary syndrome. Cerebral artery thrombosis → ischaemic stroke. Sudden occlusion = life-threatening emergency.

From the lecture slides
04

Aneurysms

Structural failure of the arterial wall.

Aneurysm

A localised, permanent dilatation of an artery, defined as a ≥50% increase in vessel diameter compared to normal. It represents structural failure of the arterial wall.

Mechanisms and causes

AtherosclerosisDegeneration of media due to plaque-induced ischaemia
HypertensionIncreases wall stress → predisposes to dissection and rupture
Infection (mycotic)Microbial destruction of the vessel wall
Connective tissue disordersMarfan syndrome — fibrillin-1 defect → weak elastic tissue. Ehlers–Danlos — defective collagen → loss of tensile strength
VasculitisInflammatory destruction, e.g. syphilitic aortitis

Major types

AtheroscleroticUsually abdominal aorta; associated with plaques and wall thinning
Dissecting (aortic dissection)Intimal tear → blood flows between layers of media; linked to hypertension or connective tissue disorders
Berry aneurysmsCongenital defects at arterial bifurcations (circle of Willis); major cause of subarachnoid haemorrhage
Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysmsHypertensive degeneration of small penetrating cerebral vessels; cause intracerebral haemorrhage
MycoticInfection weakens the wall; often secondary to septic emboli (e.g. endocarditis)
A dental link worth noticing

Mycotic aneurysms are often secondary to septic emboli from endocarditis — and viridans streptococci from dental bacteraemia are a classic cause of endocarditis, covered later in this lecture. The chain runs from an oral organism to a ruptured artery.

Two cerebral aneurysms, two bleeds

Berry → subarachnoid haemorrhage (congenital, at the circle of Willis). Charcot–Bouchard → intracerebral haemorrhage (hypertensive, small penetrating vessels). Different cause, different location, different bleed.

05

Hypertension

Definition, causes, and what it does to organs.

Hypertension

Persistently elevated arterial blood pressure. Diagnostic threshold (clinic reading) ≥140/90 mmHg; home/ambulatory thresholds are slightly lower (≥135/85) due to reduced white-coat effect. Requires sustained elevation, confirmed across multiple visits or via 24-hour ABPM.

Read this before taking a BP in the surgery

A single raised measurement in a dental clinic does not equal a diagnosis — assess for anxiety, pain, caffeine or stress. Avoid diagnosing on a single measurement unless BP is severely elevated. Evaluate in the context of comorbidities (diabetes, CKD, cardiovascular disease).

~90%

Essential (primary)

Multifactorial; no single identifiable cause. Genetic polymorphisms affecting RAAS, sodium handling and vascular tone; environmental factors — high salt intake, sedentary lifestyle, obesity → insulin resistance → sympathetic activation, chronic stress → catecholamine excess. Plus sympathetic overactivity and subclinical renal sodium retention.

~10%

Secondary

Renal: CKD, renovascular hypertension (renal artery stenosis), polycystic kidney disease. Endocrine: Conn syndrome, Cushing syndrome, phaeochromocytoma, thyroid disorders. Cardiovascular: coarctation of the aorta, aortic stiffening. Medications: NSAIDs, OCPs, corticosteroids, ciclosporin, erythropoietin.

Mechanisms of essential hypertension

  • Increased total peripheral resistance — structural narrowing of small arteries and arterioles; endothelial dysfunction reduces nitric oxide and increases vasoconstriction; vascular remodelling perpetuates resistance
  • Enhanced sympathetic nervous system activity — increased resting heart rate and vasomotor tone

Systemic effects

OrganEffects
HeartLeft ventricular hypertrophy — concentric hypertrophy from pressure overload, increased myocardial oxygen demand, reduced diastolic filling, risk of heart failure, accelerated atherosclerosis. Arrhythmias — atrial fibrillation risk rises with LVH and atrial dilation
KidneysHypertensive nephrosclerosis (hyaline arteriolosclerosis → glomerular ischaemia, falling GFR) and CKD — reduced drug clearance, electrolyte disturbance (hyperkalaemia risk, especially with RAAS inhibitors)
BrainIschaemic stroke (lacunar infarcts from small-vessel disease), intracerebral haemorrhage (rupture of Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms), vascular dementia
EyesHypertensive retinopathy — arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, cotton-wool spots, haemorrhages. In emergency: papilloedema, risk of permanent vision loss
Why LVH is a vicious circle

Pressure overload causes hypertrophy; hypertrophy increases myocardial oxygen demand while hypertension is simultaneously accelerating atherosclerosis in the coronaries that must supply it. Demand rises as supply falls — which is the definition of ischaemic heart disease later in this lecture.

06

Diabetic vascular disease

Three pathologies, one metabolic cause.

1

Accelerated atherosclerosis

Macrovascular. Earlier onset and more severe plaques, affecting coronary, carotid, cerebral and peripheral arteries.

2

Hypertensive vascular disease

Diabetes significantly increases the risk of hypertension.

3

Diabetic microangiopathy

The most characteristic feature.

Mechanisms

Accelerated atherosclerosisGlycation of lipoproteins → enhanced LDL oxidation; chronic inflammation due to advanced glycation end-products (AGEs); endothelial dysfunction → reduced nitric oxide, increased vasoconstriction
HypertensionRenal sodium retention, RAAS overactivity, sympathetic activation
MicroangiopathyThickening of capillary basement membranes, narrowed lumen → impaired perfusion, with microaneurysms, leakage and haemorrhages, ischaemia

Microangiopathy affects the small vessels of the retina, kidney glomeruli, vasa nervorum (peripheral nerves), and skin and mucosa.

Clinical consequences

Diabetic nephropathy — leading cause of dialysis worldwide Retinopathy — non-proliferative then proliferative, risking blindness Neuropathy — sensory loss → foot ulcers; autonomic → arrhythmias, gastroparesis Poor wound healing
Poor wound healing — three mechanisms at once

Reduced perfusion, impaired neutrophil function, and increased infection risk. Exactly the convergence Lecture 4 identified as making diabetes the classic example of impaired healing — and it explains slow extraction-socket healing and periodontal disease severity in diabetic patients.

Dental relevance

Reduced healing from poor perfusion; increased MI and stroke risk during stress; careful vasoconstrictor use; BP monitoring essential; avoid elective care in uncontrolled hypertension; adjust drug doses if renal impairment is present. And neuropathy blunts oral pain response, so a diabetic patient may under-report a significant problem.

07

Vasculitis and giant cell arteritis

Inflammation of the vessel wall — and one with a jaw sign.

Vasculitis

Inflammatory destruction of blood vessel walls, leading to structural weakness, narrowing or occlusion. Can involve arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules or veins depending on subtype.

Vessel sizeInvolvesExamples
LargeMajor elastic arteries (aorta and primary branches)Giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis
MediumMuscular arteries supplying major organsPolyarteritis nodosa, Kawasaki disease
SmallArterioles, capillaries, venulesANCA-associated vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis), immune complex vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura), microscopic polyangiitis

Pathogenic mechanisms

ANCA antibodies (PR3-ANCA, MPO-ANCA) T cell–mediated inflammation Immune complex deposition — post-infectious, SLE Infectious — hepatitis B/C, bacterial or fungal
Lecture 5 again

Immune complex deposition is type III hypersensitivity, and SLE is named as a cause — exactly the multi-system deposition disease from L5A. T cell–mediated vasculitis is type IV. Vasculitis is hypersensitivity localised to vessel walls.

Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis)

  • Occurs almost exclusively in older adults (>50 years); more common in females; associated with polymyalgia rheumatica
  • Headache localised to the temporal regions, due to granulomatous inflammation of the temporal artery
  • Jaw claudication — pain or fatigue of the jaw muscles during chewing, caused by ischaemia of the masseter and pterygoid muscles
  • Scalp tenderness — pain when brushing hair or touching the scalp
  • Visual disturbances — amaurosis fugax, blurred vision, diplopia
  • Systemic: fever, weight loss, malaise
Jaw claudication is a dental emergency, not a TMD

Giant cell arteritis carries a risk of irreversible blindness due to occlusion of the ophthalmic artery. An older patient with jaw pain on chewing, temporal headache and scalp tenderness is not presenting with temporomandibular dysfunction — this needs urgent referral, because the visual loss is preventable but not reversible.

A 72-year-old reports jaw pain that comes on while chewing and eases with rest, plus a temporal headache. Why is this urgent?

This is jaw claudication — pain or fatigue of the jaw muscles during chewing from ischaemia of the masseter and pterygoid muscles — a cardinal feature of giant cell arteritis. The urgency is the risk of irreversible blindness from occlusion of the ophthalmic artery. Look also for scalp tenderness, visual disturbance (amaurosis fugax, diplopia) and systemic symptoms, and refer immediately.

From the lecture slides
08

Heart failure

Left and right, and why they present so differently.

Heart failure

Inability of the heart to pump sufficient blood to meet metabolic demands. May result from impaired ventricular filling (diastolic dysfunction) or impaired contraction (systolic dysfunction), and is typically associated with neurohormonal activation (SNS, RAAS) leading to fluid retention and vascular congestion.

FeatureLeft-sidedRight-sided
Primary dysfunctionLV cannot pump blood forward → reduced cardiac outputRV cannot pump into the pulmonary circulation → systemic venous congestion
Main causesIschaemic heart disease, hypertension, aortic/mitral valve disease, cardiomyopathyLeft-sided HF (most common), pulmonary hypertension, chronic lung disease (cor pulmonale), pulmonary embolism
Haemodynamics↑ pulmonary venous pressure → pulmonary congestion↑ systemic venous pressure → oedema and organ congestion
SymptomsDyspnoea (exertional → rest), orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, fatigue, weaknessPeripheral oedema, hepatomegaly, ascites, jugular venous distension, abdominal discomfort
SignsTachypnoea, crackles on auscultation, cyanosis (late)Pitting oedema, liver tenderness, elevated JVP, weight gain from fluid retention
PathologyLV dilation or hypertrophy, pulmonary oedema, haemosiderin-laden “heart failure cells”Congested liver (“nutmeg liver”), systemic venous congestion, serous effusions

Congestive heart failure is combined left + right failure, most common in advanced or chronic disease, with widespread oedema, fatigue and severe exercise intolerance.

The commonest cause of right heart failure is left heart failure

Blood backs up through the lungs into the right side. That is why isolated right-sided failure is rare unless it is driven by lung disease — cor pulmonale.

Dental considerations

Semi-upright positioning is essential — a left-sided failure patient cannot tolerate lying flat and desaturates rapidly during long procedures. Keep appointments short and stress-free, avoid excess vasoconstrictor, and monitor oxygen saturation. In right-sided failure, hepatic congestion reduces drug metabolism, so adjust doses of liver-metabolised drugs, and watch for hypotension when reclining.

From the lecture slides
09

Ischaemic heart disease and acute coronary syndromes

One spectrum, four presentations.

Ischaemic heart disease

A mismatch between myocardial oxygen supply and demand — from reduced coronary perfusion, increased metabolic demand, or both. The primary cause is coronary atherosclerosis (~90% of cases). Other contributors: coronary vasospasm (Prinzmetal angina), and anaemia, hypotension and tachyarrhythmias as secondary ischaemia.

ConditionMechanismPattern
Stable anginaFixed atherosclerotic narrowing (>70% lumen reduction); coronaries cannot dilate enough to meet demandPredictable chest pain on exertion or stress; relieved by rest or nitrates
Unstable anginaPlaque rupture, platelet aggregation, non-occlusive thrombusPain increasing in frequency or severity, at rest or minimal exertion; a pre-infarction state requiring urgent assessment
Myocardial infarctionAcute plaque rupture → thrombosis → complete or near-complete occlusion → severe sustained ischaemiaProlonged ischaemia → irreversible myocyte necrosis, with characteristic troponin elevation
Sudden cardiac deathFatal arrhythmia, typically ventricular fibrillationUnexpected cardiac arrest within 1 hour of symptom onset; may be the first clinical presentation
Stable vs unstable, in one line

Stable angina is a supply-and-demand problem across a fixed narrowing — predictable, exertional, relieved by rest. Unstable angina is a ruptured plaque — unpredictable, at rest, and not relieved by rest. The change in pattern is what signals the change in pathology.

Consequences of MI

Arrhythmias, and ventricular fibrillation as the most common cause of early death. Sudden cardiac death is triggered by acute ischaemia, structural heart disease (cardiomyopathy, valve disease) or electrical instability, with coronary atherosclerosis present in the majority of cases.

A patient with long-standing stable angina now gets chest pain at rest that is not relieved by rest. What has changed?

The pathology has changed from a fixed stenosis to a ruptured plaque. Stable angina is demand-driven ischaemia across fixed narrowing, relieved by rest because rest reduces demand. Pain at rest or minimal exertion, increasing in frequency or severity, indicates unstable angina — plaque rupture with platelet aggregation and non-occlusive thrombus. This is an acute coronary syndrome and a pre-infarction state requiring urgent medical assessment, not elective dental treatment.

From the lecture slides
10

Valvular disease and infective endocarditis

The section where dentistry matters most.

Major causes of valvular disease

Rheumatic heart diseasePost-streptococcal autoimmune reaction causing leaflet thickening, commissural fusion and chordae shortening; classically affects the mitral valve, sometimes aortic
Degenerative (calcific)Age-related fibrosis and calcification; the most common cause of aortic stenosis
Rheumatic heart disease is cross-reactivity

Lecture 5A gave this as the classic example of molecular mimicry — antibodies raised against streptococcal antigens also bind cardiac tissue because the two are structurally similar. This is the valve damage that results, and it is why those patients then need endocarditis risk management for life.

Infective endocarditis

Definition

Infection of cardiac valves or endocardial surfaces. Commonly caused by viridans streptococci (classically after dental bacteraemia), Staphylococcus aureus (acute, aggressive), and enterococci.

High-risk groups

Prosthetic valves Prior infective endocarditis Certain congenital heart disease
Why this is the single most dentally relevant item in the lecture

Viridans streptococci are oral commensals, and the classic route is dental bacteraemia. That is the entire basis of antibiotic prophylaxis policy for high-risk cardiac patients. Note the risk is concentrated in a defined group — prosthetic valves, previous endocarditis, and certain congenital heart disease — not in everyone with a murmur.

Congenital heart disease

Structural cardiac abnormalities present at birth, affecting septa, valves, major vessels or conduction pathways.

Ventricular septal defect (VSD)Most common congenital defect; left-to-right shunt → pulmonary hypertension in severe cases
Atrial septal defect (ASD)Often asymptomatic early
11

Haemostasis

Primary, secondary, and the brakes on both.

Primary

The platelet plug

  • Triggered by endothelial injury exposing subendothelial collagen and von Willebrand factor (vWF)
  • Platelet adhesion via vWF–GPIb interaction
  • Activation: shape change, granule release (ADP, TXA2, serotonin), expression of activated GPIIb/IIIa
Secondary

The coagulation cascade

  • Extrinsic pathway: tissue factor activates factor VII → rapid response
  • Intrinsic pathway: contact activation → factors XII, XI, IX, VIII
  • Both converge on the common pathway (X → Xa → II → IIa → fibrin)
  • Thrombin = central amplifier of coagulation

Natural anticoagulants: protein C, protein S, antithrombin. Plus fibrinolysis for clot breakdown.

Vitamin K–dependent factors

II, VII, IX, X (plus proteins C and S). These are the factors warfarin depletes — which is why warfarin affects both the extrinsic (VII) and intrinsic/common pathways, and why its effect is monitored by INR.

Two haemostasis defects give two bleeding patterns

Primary haemostasis failure (platelets, vWF) gives mucocutaneous bleeding — petechiae, gingival oozing, epistaxis. Secondary failure (coagulation factors) gives deep bleeding — haemarthroses and muscle haematomas. Recognising which pattern a patient reports tells you which arm is defective.

From the lecture slides
12

Thrombocytopenia

Too few platelets — three mechanisms.

Thrombocytopenia

Platelet count <150 × 109/L. Severe thrombocytopenia (<20 × 109/L) causes spontaneous bleeding and risk of life-threatening haemorrhage.

1

Decreased production

Bone marrow suppression or failure.

2

Increased destruction

Immune or non-immune mechanisms.

3

Increased sequestration

Splenic pooling.

Causes of reduced production

Megaloblastic anaemiaVitamin B12 or folate deficiency → ineffective DNA synthesis → impaired marrow maturation, reducing output of RBCs, WBCs and platelets
Bone marrow infiltrationLeukaemia (especially acute forms), lymphoma, metastatic cancer, fibrosis — displacing normal marrow
The number to remember

<20 × 109/L is the threshold for spontaneous bleeding. Below it, a patient can bleed without trauma — and any dental intervention becomes significantly higher risk. Above roughly 50, most routine dentistry is manageable, but check current counts rather than assuming.

B12/folate deficiency has an oral face too

Megaloblastic anaemia reduces all three cell lines. The same deficiencies appeared in Lecture 6 as causes of angular cheilitis, and they produce glossitis and mucosal atrophy — so an oral finding may be the first clue to a haematological problem.

From the lecture slides
13

von Willebrand disease and haemophilia

The commonest inherited bleeding disorder, and the classic ones.

von Willebrand disease

  • Most common inherited bleeding disorder (~1% of population)
  • Caused by quantitative or qualitative defects in vWF
  • vWF has two roles: mediates platelet adhesion via GPIb, and stabilises and carries Factor VIII in circulation
  • Bleeding pattern resembles a platelet-type disorder because primary haemostasis is impaired
One protein, two jobs — so two possible pictures

Because vWF carries Factor VIII, losing it also lowers Factor VIII. But the dominant clinical picture is platelet-type — mucocutaneous bleeding — because the adhesion role fails first. That dual function is what makes vWD sit between the primary and secondary categories.

Haemophilia A and B

 Haemophilia AHaemophilia B
DeficiencyFactor VIIIFactor IX
Proportion80–85% of haemophilia casesThe remainder
ReplacementFactor VIII replacementFactor IX replacement

Clinical features

  • Haemarthroses (joint bleeding) — knees, ankles, elbows most affected; repeated bleeds cause synovial hypertrophy, cartilage loss, chronic arthropathy
  • Deep muscle haematomas — iliopsoas bleeds may compromise nerves or vessels and may mimic an acute abdomen
  • Prolonged bleeding after dental procedures

Management

On-demand therapy for bleeds; regular prophylaxis to prevent haemarthroses in severe disease. Emerging: gene therapy, and emicizumab for haemophilia A — a Factor VIII mimetic that bypasses the missing factor.

Other factor deficiencies

XI

Factor XI deficiency

Common in Ashkenazi Jewish populations; variable bleeding tendency; surgical bleeding more common than spontaneous bleeding.

XII

Factor XII deficiency

Prolonged APTT but no bleeding tendency. Do not confuse prolonged APTT with bleeding risk.

A lab result that misleads

Factor XII deficiency gives a prolonged APTT with no bleeding tendency — and is associated with thrombosis rather than haemorrhage. Treating the number rather than the patient would be exactly wrong here.

14

Liver disease and anticoagulants

Acquired bleeding problems — the ones you will actually meet.

Liver disease and coagulation

  • ↓ Synthesis of clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X, V, XI)
  • ↓ Production of fibrinogen, or dysfunctional fibrinogen
  • ↓ Clearance of activated clotting factors → paradoxical thrombosis
  • Thrombocytopenia due to hypersplenism (portal hypertension)
  • ↓ Vitamin K absorption in cholestasis
Liver disease is not simply “bleeding risk”

It reduces both pro- and anticoagulant factors, and reduced clearance of activated factors can cause paradoxical thrombosis. The balance is unstable in both directions, which is why these patients need individual assessment rather than a rule of thumb.

Anticoagulant drugs

DrugMechanismClinical notes
WarfarinInhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, depleting factors II, VII, IX, XRequires INR monitoring; many drug and diet interactions; stop or adjust only on medical advice
DOACsDirect inhibition of thrombin or factor XaNo routine monitoring; shorter half-life
AntiplateletsInhibit platelet activation/aggregationAffect primary haemostasis
Two interactions from earlier lectures

Miconazole potentiates warfarin (Lecture 6) — a topical antifungal you might prescribe routinely. And warfarin depends on the vitamin K–dependent factors II, VII, IX, X, which is why cholestatic liver disease compounds the effect by reducing vitamin K absorption.

A patient on warfarin needs an extraction. Why is checking the INR more useful than asking about their dose?

Because warfarin's effect depends on depletion of the vitamin K–dependent factors II, VII, IX and X, and that depletion varies with diet, other drugs and liver function — not just dose. The lecture notes warfarin requires INR monitoring with many drug and diet interactions. The INR measures the actual current anticoagulant effect. Note also that some drugs a dentist prescribes, such as miconazole, potentiate warfarin.

From the lecture slides
15

Summary and glossary

Cardiovascular and blood on one screen.

The through-line

  1. The endothelium starts almost everything
    Injury begins atherosclerosis; dysfunction drives hypertension and diabetic vascular disease; exposure triggers haemostasis.
  2. Atherosclerosis is chronic inflammation
    Oxidised LDL as the indigestible agent, with the adhesion molecules and macrophages of Lecture 3.
  3. Vulnerable plaques are soft, not hard
    Thin cap, big lipid core, inflamed — and may not be the tightest stenosis.
  4. Hypertension damages four organs
    Heart, kidney, brain, eye — and one clinic reading is not a diagnosis.
  5. IHD is one spectrum
    Fixed stenosis → stable angina; ruptured plaque → unstable angina, MI, sudden death.
  6. Giant cell arteritis presents in the jaw
    Jaw claudication with headache in an older patient risks irreversible blindness.
  7. Endocarditis is the dental link
    Viridans streptococci, classically after dental bacteraemia, in a defined high-risk group.
  8. Two bleeding patterns, two arms
    Mucocutaneous = primary (platelets, vWF); deep = secondary (coagulation factors).

Glossary

Vasa vasorum
Small vessels supplying the outer wall of a large vessel.
Atherosclerosis
Chronic inflammatory, lipid-driven disease of large and medium arteries.
Foam cell
Macrophage that has engulfed oxidised LDL; accumulates to form fatty streaks.
Fibrous cap
Collagen-rich layer produced by smooth muscle cells, stabilising a plaque.
Vulnerable plaque
Thin-capped, lipid-rich, inflamed, less calcified plaque prone to rupture.
Aneurysm
Localised permanent dilatation of an artery, ≥50% increase in diameter.
Dissection
Intimal tear allowing blood to flow between the layers of the media.
Berry aneurysm
Congenital aneurysm at a bifurcation of the circle of Willis; causes subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysm
Hypertensive degeneration of small penetrating cerebral vessels; causes intracerebral haemorrhage.
Mycotic aneurysm
Aneurysm from microbial destruction of the wall, often from septic emboli.
Essential hypertension
Multifactorial hypertension with no single identifiable cause; ~90% of cases.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Concentric hypertrophy from chronic pressure overload.
AGEs
Advanced glycation end-products; drive chronic inflammation in diabetes.
Microangiopathy
Thickened capillary basement membranes with narrowed lumen; the characteristic diabetic vascular lesion.
Vasculitis
Inflammatory destruction of blood vessel walls.
Jaw claudication
Pain or fatigue of the jaw muscles on chewing, from ischaemia of masseter and pterygoids; a feature of giant cell arteritis.
Cor pulmonale
Right heart failure secondary to chronic lung disease.
Orthopnoea
Breathlessness on lying flat.
Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea
Sudden nocturnal breathlessness waking the patient.
Nutmeg liver
Mottled congested liver of right-sided heart failure.
Prinzmetal angina
Angina from coronary vasospasm rather than fixed stenosis.
Troponin
Biomarker elevated in myocardial infarction.
Infective endocarditis
Infection of cardiac valves or endocardial surfaces; classically viridans streptococci after dental bacteraemia.
vWF
von Willebrand factor; mediates platelet adhesion via GPIb and carries Factor VIII.
Haemarthrosis
Bleeding into a joint; characteristic of haemophilia.
Thrombocytopenia
Platelet count <150 × 109/L; spontaneous bleeding below 20.
Emicizumab
Factor VIII mimetic bypassing the missing factor in haemophilia A.
Required reading

Underwood’s Pathology: a Clinical Approach (8th ed.), Simon Cross (2024), Chapter 13 — Cardiovascular System, and Chapter 23 — Blood and Bone Marrow: disorders of blood coagulation and haemostasis.
